Click3R: Interactive Stereo 3D Reconstruction with Sparse Correspondence Clicks

Hao Gu*†    Jin Yao*    Zezhou Cheng Affiliation: University of Virginia Affiliation: uva-computer-vision-lab.github.io/click3r
Abstract

Despite impressive progress, existing feed-forward large 3D reconstruction models produce a single, irrevocable prediction. When these models fail, there is no mechanism to correct their mistakes. To address this limitation, we introduce Click3R, a framework for interactive geometric correction of feed-forward models using sparse human correspondence clicks. Given an image pair and a small set of cross-view point correspondences provided by a user, Click3R injects geometric constraints into the 3D reconstruction networks through a lightweight point correspondence adapter, enabling the model to resolve ambiguities in challenging scenarios such as repetitive textures, symmetric structures, large viewpoint changes, or textureless regions. To evaluate interactive reconstruction, we curate a challenging benchmark specifically designed to expose failure modes of existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods. Experiments show that Click3R reduces reconstruction error with as few as a single correspondence click, improving performance on both standard and our curated benchmarks. Our results highlight that sparse human interaction provides an effective and practical mechanism for correcting geometric reconstruction errors.

††footnotetext: ∗Equal contribution.  †Project lead.

1 Introduction

Feed-forward stereo 3D reconstruction methods [44, 16, 29, 49] have transformed multi-view geometry by replacing iterative optimization [25, 34] with direct regression. Given two images, these models predict dense 3D pointmaps in a single forward pass, achieving remarkable speed and generalization across diverse scenes. This paradigm has recently been extended to multi-view settings [42, 45, 53, 40, 3]. Despite their impressive performance, the efficiency comes at a fundamental cost: when the prediction is wrong, there is no simple mechanism to correct it. Unlike optimization-based methods [34] that iteratively refine their estimates using geometric constraints, feed-forward models produce a single, irrevocable output and fail silently, particularly on challenging scenes with repetitive textures, symmetric structures, or extreme viewpoint changes (Fig. 1a,b).

Several approaches aim to improve the reliability of feed-forward reconstruction models through test-time optimization [24, 5]. For instance, LoRA3D [24] introduces a self-calibration pipeline that fine-tunes a pretrained DUSt3R model [44] to a target scene. Although these methods improve performance, iterative test-time optimization is computationally expensive and, more importantly, cannot resolve failures when the model encounters genuinely ambiguous scenes at inference time. Another line of work improves robustness by incorporating auxiliary geometric priors. For example, Pow3R [10] shows that conditioning on camera intrinsics, relative camera poses, or depth maps can significantly improve reconstruction performance. However, such auxiliary information is often unavailable in practice. Meanwhile, classical reconstruction methods have long relied on explicit correspondences as geometric constraints [34, 31, 22]. Unfortunately, automatically estimated correspondences remain unreliable in scenarios with repetitive textures or large viewpoint changes.

Nevertheless, cross-view correspondences, even just a handful of point pairs, carry powerful geometric information: they constrain the epipolar geometry, resolve depth ambiguities, and disambiguate symmetric structures. This motivates a simple question: can sparse human-provided correspondences guide feed-forward 3D reconstruction models without sacrificing the efficiency of the feed-forward paradigm? Instead of relying solely on feed-forward models or automatically estimated correspondences, we allow the user to manually provide a small set of cross-view point correspondences (Fig. 1a), when the model produces unsatisfactory reconstructions.

To unlock this capability, we introduce Click3R, a lightweight framework that incorporates user-provided correspondences into feed-forward 3D reconstruction, enabling interactive geometric correction without test-time model fine-tuning or optimization. Specifically, Click3R employs a simple correspondence adapter that injects the geometric constraints imposed by user clicks into the reconstruction network via a cross-attention mechanism (Fig. 2). We train the base model and the adapter jointly end-to-end on widely used 3D datasets [28, 2, 57] using simulated human clicks. During training, the number of clicks is randomly sampled to expose the model to varying levels of user interaction, enabling it to operate under different levels of click sparsity at test time.

To systematically evaluate the proposed interactive reconstruction, we further introduce Hard3DBench, a benchmark designed to expose failure modes of state-of-the-art feed-forward reconstruction models. The benchmark contains image pairs and 5-view tuples with ground-truth 3D reconstructions, exhibiting challenging conditions (large viewpoint changes, low overlap, large baselines, extreme depth ranges) where feed-forward reconstruction models often struggle. Our experiments demonstrate that Click3R consistently outperforms baseline methods, particularly on challenging scenarios from Hard3DBench (Fig. 1c).

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose Click3R, which injects sparse human correspondence clicks into feed-forward stereo 3D reconstruction networks via a lightweight correspondence adapter.

  • •

    We curate Hard3DBench, a diagnostic benchmark with a detailed failure taxonomy under which current feed-forward reconstruction models degrade substantially relative to standard evaluation samples.

  • •

    We show that Click3R dramatically improves reconstruction accuracy on challenging cases. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on interactive stereo feed-forward 3D reconstruction using sparse correspondence clicks.

2 Related Work

Feed-Forward Stereo 3D Reconstruction.

DUSt3R [44] pioneered dense 3D pointmap regression from image pairs using a CroCo-pretrained [48, 47] ViT encoder-decoder, bypassing explicit matching and triangulation. MASt3R [16] extended this with dense local feature heads. The paradigm has rapidly advanced toward multi-view: Spann3R [41] and MUSt3R [3] use spatial memory across frames; CUT3R [43] employs a recurrent model with persistent state; Fast3R [53] scales to 1000+ images in a single forward pass; and VGGT [42] and Pi3 [45] predict from arbitrary views with a single Transformer. Despite their diversity, all these methods rely solely on learned visual priors and cannot incorporate external geometric evidence at inference. Our work is orthogonal: Click3R augments feed-forward stereo reconstruction with sparse correspondence guidance.

Conditioned 3D Reconstruction.

Several concurrent methods condition feed-forward 3D models on external geometric signals: Pow3R [10] on camera intrinsics, depth, or pose, G-CUT3R [14] on camera and depth modalities, Rig3R [17] on multi-camera rig metadata, and Mono3R [18] on monocular depth. MapAnything [13] unifies a flexible mix of conditioning inputs (intrinsics, poses, depth, partial reconstructions) into a single feed-forward model, while Any4D [12] extends conditional reconstruction to dynamic 4D scenes with multi-modal sensor inputs. In the depth estimation domain, PromptDA [21] prompts Depth Anything [54] with sparse LiDAR points. All these methods condition on scene-level priors that improve metric accuracy but cannot resolve perceptual aliasing. To our knowledge, Click3R is the first to introduce correspondence prompting, which conditions feed-forward 3D reconstruction on cross-view point correspondences that directly disambiguate geometric ambiguities, analogous to SAM’s [15, 27] click-based segmentation prompting.

Interactive Vision System.

Interactive segmentation has a long history of incorporating user guidance into visual recognition. Early methods use bounding boxes [30] or scribbles [20], while recent approaches adopt click-based prompting [51, 4, 23, 39], culminating in SAM [15, 27]. Beyond segmentation, point-based interaction has been extended to image editing: DragGAN [26] and DragDiffusion [37] enable users to manipulate content by dragging points. Recent work has also explored interactive guidance for 3D reconstruction; for example, Toon3D [46] uses sparse user annotations for cartoon 3D reconstruction. However, these interactive paradigms have largely remained confined to 2D tasks or stylized 3D settings. Early interactive systems also explored correspondence-based 3D reconstruction [9]. Click3R brings this idea to feed-forward stereo models, with point correspondences as geometric constraints rather than semantic cues.

3 Methodology

Given an image pair (I1,I2)(I_{1},I_{2}) and an optional set of sparse point correspondences 𝒞={(𝐩i1,𝐩i2)}i=1K\mathcal{C}=\{(\mathbf{p}_{i}^{1},\mathbf{p}_{i}^{2})\}_{i=1}^{K}, where 𝐩iv∈ℝ2\mathbf{p}_{i}^{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} denotes the pixel coordinates in view vv, Click3R predicts dense 3D pointmaps for both views. When no correspondences are provided, the adapter reduces to an identity mapping, and the model behaves identically to the base reconstruction model without prompts. An overview of the Click3R architecture is shown in Fig. 2.

3.1 Preliminaries: DUSt3R

DUSt3R [44] uses a shared ViT-Large encoder (Denc=1024D_{\text{enc}}=1024, 24 blocks) to process each image independently, followed by an asymmetric decoder (Ddec=768D_{\text{dec}}=768, 12 blocks per branch) with cross-attention between views. The encoder produces patch tokens

𝐅v=Encoder​(Iv)∈ℝN×Denc,N=Hp×Wp,\mathbf{F}_{v}=\text{Encoder}(I_{v})\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D_{\text{enc}}},\quad N=\tfrac{H}{p}\times\tfrac{W}{p}, (1)

where pp is the patch size. Tokens are projected to decoder dimension, 𝐆v=proj​(𝐅v)∈ℝN×Ddec\mathbf{G}_{v}=\text{proj}(\mathbf{F}_{v})\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D_{\text{dec}}}, then processed by interleaved self- and cross-attention blocks. A linear prediction head maps the decoded tokens to dense 3D pointmaps X^v∈ℝH×W×3\hat{X}_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} and confidence maps C^v∈ℝH×W\hat{C}_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} in view 1’s frame.

Click3R inserts its correspondence adapter after this projection and before the first decoder block, modifying 𝐆v\mathbf{G}_{v} using sparse correspondence prompts. The base model and adapter are trained jointly end-to-end.

3.2 Correspondence Tokenizer

Our tokenizer converts sparse correspondences into tokens for cross-attention with image features. For each correspondence point 𝐩iv=(xi,yi)\mathbf{p}_{i}^{v}=(x_{i},y_{i}), we normalize its coordinates to the token grid:

𝐩¯iv=(xi/pwWt−1,yi/phHt−1),\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{i}^{v}=\left(\frac{x_{i}/p_{w}}{W_{t}-1},\ \frac{y_{i}/p_{h}}{H_{t}-1}\right), (2)

clipped to [0,1][0,1], where pw,php_{w},p_{h} are effective patch sizes and Wt,HtW_{t},H_{t} are token-grid dimensions; this is the scale on which the image positional encoding places token jj at j/(Wt−1)j/(W_{t}-1). We encode the normalized point using SAM-style random Fourier features [15]:

𝐞pos​(𝐩¯iv)=[sin⁡(2​π​𝐁​(2​𝐩¯iv−1));cos⁡(2​π​𝐁​(2​𝐩¯iv−1))]∈ℝD,\mathbf{e}_{\text{pos}}(\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{i}^{v})=[\sin(2\pi\mathbf{B}(2\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{i}^{v}-1));\ \cos(2\pi\mathbf{B}(2\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{i}^{v}-1))]\in\mathbb{R}^{D}, (3)

with fixed Gaussian matrix 𝐁∈ℝD/2×2\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{D/2\times 2}, preserving sub-pixel precision.

To identify the view and to link matched points across views, we add a learnable image embedding 𝐞img​(v)∈ℝD\mathbf{e}_{\text{img}}(v)\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and a learnable pair embedding 𝐞pair​(i)∈ℝD\mathbf{e}_{\text{pair}}(i)\in\mathbb{R}^{D} shared by both points in the same correspondence. The final token is

𝐭iv=𝐞pos​(𝐩¯iv)+𝐞img​(v)+𝐞pair​(i)∈ℝD.\mathbf{t}_{i}^{v}=\mathbf{e}_{\text{pos}}(\bar{\mathbf{p}}_{i}^{v})+\mathbf{e}_{\text{img}}(v)+\mathbf{e}_{\text{pair}}(i)\in\mathbb{R}^{D}. (4)

For each view, visible correspondence tokens form 𝐓v∈ℝKv×D\mathbf{T}_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{K_{v}\times D}. The tokenizer is shared across both view adapters.

3.3 Point Correspondence Adapter

We inject correspondence information into DUSt3R’s decoder using a two-way attention adapter inspired by SAM [15], enabling bidirectional exchange between sparse correspondence tokens and dense image tokens (Figure 2).

Two-Way Attention.

The adapter has L=2L=2 layers. Each layer applies: (1) self-attention over prompt tokens 𝐓v\mathbf{T}_{v}; (2) prompt-to-image cross-attention, Attn​(𝐓v,𝐆v,𝐆v)\text{Attn}(\mathbf{T}_{v},\mathbf{G}_{v},\mathbf{G}_{v}); (3) an MLP on prompt tokens; and (4) image-to-prompt cross-attention, Attn​(𝐆v,𝐓v,𝐓v)\text{Attn}(\mathbf{G}_{v},\mathbf{T}_{v},\mathbf{T}_{v}). This bidirectional design lets prompts condition image features with correspondence constraints while allowing prompt tokens to absorb local visual context.

Image Positional Encoding.

For cross-attention, image positional encodings are computed by applying the same Fourier PE to normalized DUSt3R token-grid positions. Thus, prompt and image tokens share a common coordinate space, allowing cross-attention to compare their spatial locations consistently.

Asymmetric Design.

We employ independent adapters 𝒜1,𝒜2\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2} for view 1 and view 2, each with a separate two-way attention adapter but sharing the same correspondence tokenizer:

𝐆1′\displaystyle\mathbf{G}_{1}^{\prime} =𝒜1​(𝐆1,𝐓1,pos1)\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}_{1}(\mathbf{G}_{1},\ \mathbf{T}_{1},\ \text{pos}_{1}) (5)
𝐆2′\displaystyle\mathbf{G}_{2}^{\prime} =𝒜2​(𝐆2,𝐓2,pos2)\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}_{2}(\mathbf{G}_{2},\ \mathbf{T}_{2},\ \text{pos}_{2}) (6)

This reflects DUSt3R’s asymmetric decoder, where each view has a separate branch. When no prompts are provided (K=0K=0, 𝐓v=∅\mathbf{T}_{v}=\varnothing), the adapter reduces to an identity mapping: 𝐆v′=𝐆v\mathbf{G}_{v}^{\prime}=\mathbf{G}_{v}.

3.4 Training Details

We use DUSt3R’s confidence-weighted regression loss:

ℒ=∑v∈{1,2}∑𝐱Cv​(𝐱)⋅‖X^v​(𝐱)−Xv∗​(𝐱)‖2−α​log⁡Cv​(𝐱)\mathcal{L}=\sum_{v\in\{1,2\}}\sum_{\mathbf{x}}C_{v}(\mathbf{x})\cdot\|\hat{X}_{v}(\mathbf{x})-X_{v}^{*}(\mathbf{x})\|_{2}-\alpha\log C_{v}(\mathbf{x}) (7)

where CvC_{v} is predicted confidence, X^v\hat{X}_{v} and Xv∗X_{v}^{*} are predicted and ground-truth pointmaps, and α=0.2\alpha\!=\!0.2. The loss is computed in a scale invariant manner.

We generate training prompts from ground-truth 3D geometry by sampling a curriculum over the number of correspondences and keeping only mutually visible correspondences. See more training and prompt generation details in B.

4 Hard3DBench

The primary value of Click3R is on challenging scenarios where DUSt3R fails. Standard evaluations report only aggregate metrics, masking catastrophic failures on geometrically ambiguous scenes. To enable systematic analysis, we introduce Hard3DBench, a curated benchmark for both 2-view stereo and 5-view multi-view settings, accompanied by a failure taxonomy that exposes the specific failure modes of feed-forward 3D reconstruction. The 2-view setting contains 404 in-distribution and 300 out-of-distribution pairs, and the 5-view setting 400 in-distribution and 300 out-of-distribution tuples. In-distribution samples come from held-out test/validation splits of four datasets used to train DUSt3R and Click3R: BlendedMVS [56], CO3D [28], Habitat [32], and WildRGB-D [50]. Out-of-distribution samples come from five datasets absent from training: 7Scenes [38], DTU [11], ETH3D [35], NRGBD [1], and ScanNet [6]. Full curation details are in Appendix C.

Failure Taxonomy.

We identify five primary failure modes in the 2-view subset (Figure 3): large viewpoint change (>60∘>60^{\circ}), moderate viewpoint change (30∘30^{\circ}–60∘60^{\circ}), low overlap (<20%<20\%), large baseline, and extreme depth range. These categories capture geometric conditions that make correspondence estimation and pose recovery difficult, such as reduced visual matches, amplified triangulation error, and increased ambiguity. Since each category is computed from ground-truth poses and depth, challenging pairs can be classified automatically without manual annotation.

5 Experiments

5.1 Evaluation Setup

Baselines.

We compare against state-of-the-art pairwise 3D reconstruction methods: (1) DUSt3R [44], the original pretrained model; (2) DUSt3R (re-trained), the same architecture re-trained on the same data as Click3R to isolate the effect of prompting from additional training data; (3) MASt3R [16], which extends DUSt3R with dense local feature matching heads; (4) VGGT [42], a feed-forward vision foundation model for 3D geometry tasks; and (5) Pi3/Pi3X [45], a permutation-equivariant multi-view reconstruction model. VGGT and Pi3/Pi3X use larger architectures and are trained on much more data, including proprietary internal datasets, with much higher computational budgets. We therefore include them as reference rather than apples-to-apples baselines.

Datasets.

For standard evaluation, we use held-out splits of three benchmarks: CO3D [28], ScanNet++ [57], and ARKitScenes [2]. For each dataset, we sample 1,000 image pairs with a fixed random seed and use the same pairs across all methods. We additionally evaluate on the Hard3DBench benchmark (Section 5.3).

Metrics.

Following DUSt3R [44], we report two metrics: scale-and-shift-invariant pointmap error for 3D reconstruction quality (lower is better) and mean Average Accuracy at threshold θ∘\theta^{\circ} (mAA@θ\theta, higher is better) for relative camera pose accuracy. Tables report mAA@30°; results at 5° and 15° are in Appendix E.2. Implementation details are in Appendix A.

Prompt selection strategies.

We evaluate several prompt selection strategies. (a) Random oracle (KKp_bestBB): sample KK correspondences BB independent times and select the set that minimizes reconstruction loss. If there’s no bestBB mentioned, KK correspondences are sampled randomly. (b) Grid oracle: partition view 1 into a 16×1616\times 16 grid of 14-pixel cells (∼\sim256 cells), select one random correspondence per populated cell, run a batched forward pass for each candidate, and keep the single correspondence whose cell yields the greatest pose improvement (reduction in max⁡(Rerr,Terr)\max(R_{\mathrm{err}},T_{\mathrm{err}})) over the no-prompt baseline. Samples without valid correspondences fall back to the no-prompt result.

5.2 Evaluation on Standard Benchmark

Table 1 presents results on standard benchmarks. Without prompts, Click3R performs on par with DUSt3R (retrained). Adding even a single well-chosen prompt (1p_best5) consistently improves over the unprompted baseline. The grid oracle reveals substantially larger headroom, with a striking +8.5%+8.5\% mAA@30° on ARKitScenes (from 84.27% to 92.75%). This confirms that prompt location matters significantly: the model can leverage even a single correspondence to meaningfully reduce pose error when placed in the right region. Notably, the grid oracle delivers the largest pose gains while pointmap error improves only modestly, indicating that prompts primarily reshape the overall scene configuration rather than uniformly tightening local surface fits.

5.3 Evaluation on Hard3DBench

Table 2 reports results on both the 2-view and 5-view subsets. Click3R consistently improves mAA@30° over the retrained DUSt3R baseline across all four conditions, with the largest gain of +9.9+9.9 on the 5-view in-distribution split, and pointmap error also improving in all four conditions. Notably, these improvements are obtained without increasing input resolution or training data. These results suggest that even sparse correspondence prompts effectively resolve failure modes in highly ambiguous scenes, enabling the model to recover accurate geometry where fully automatic methods struggle. Figure 4 shows qualitative comparisons: a few correspondence clicks placed in geometrically ambiguous regions resolve failures that produce dramatically incorrect geometry in DUSt3R. See Per-Category Analysis in Appendix Appendix D.

5.4 Evaluation with Human-Labeled Correspondences

The previous experiments use ground-truth correspondences derived from known 3D geometry. To evaluate Click3R under realistic annotation conditions, we test on 100 image pairs with human-labeled correspondences. The pairs are drawn from out-of-distribution set of Hard3DBench and cover challenging geometric configurations. A human annotator, not specifically familiar with the evaluated datasets or scenes, freely chooses sparse correspondences (3.8 per pair on average, from 1 to 7) via a labeling interface (Figure 12), without access to ground-truth depth or camera parameters.

Table 3 demonstrates that human-provided prompts drastically reduce median rotation error compared to the unprompted model (8.78° vs. 17.30°) and raise mAA@30 from 36.2 to 56.2, along with significant improvement in Relative Rotation Accuracy. Compared to the random ground-truth oracle (K=4K\!=\!4), human labels recover about 96% of the medRRE improvement gap, showing that sparse, imperfect human clicks capture most of the benefit of perfect correspondences. These results confirm that Click3R translates effectively from synthetic oracle prompts to practical human interaction.

5.5 Ablation Study

Training strategy ablation.

We compare three training strategies for Click3R: (i) freezing the DUSt3R backbone and training only the adapter, (ii) finetuning DUSt3R jointly with the adapter, and (iii) training the full pipeline from CroCo v2 [47] initialization. Averaged over the three standard benchmarks and both Hard3DBench 2-view splits with one GT click (Appendix E.1), training from CroCo v2 performs best (mAA@30 75.1%), followed by DUSt3R finetuning (72.3%), while freezing DUSt3R gives the weakest results (71.2%). This suggests that Click3R requires substantial end-to-end adaptation to align backbone features with correspondence-conditioned reasoning; training the adapter alone is insufficient.

Correspondence perturbation analysis.

To study how the model uses sparse correspondence hints, we perturb a single correspondence by fixing the click in view 1 and shifting its matched point in view 2 along a random direction. As perturbation increases, model confidence consistently decreases, indicating sensitivity to correspondence reliability (Fig. 5(a)).

We further measure whether predictions follow the true or perturbed correspondence by computing the 3D distance between predicted points at the ground-truth correspondence locations in both views. The model remains largely robust to small perturbations, but becomes more sensitive once perturbations reach half a patch (8 pixels), leading to larger degradation (Fig. 5(b)). For more analysis on how correspondences affects the adapters and downstream tasks, see Appendix F.

We also refer readers to our analyses of the effect of the number of prompts (Section E.3), robustness to image augmentation (Section E.4), and error distribution (Section E.8).

6 Conclusion

We presented Click3R, an interactive stereo 3D reconstruction framework that bridges fully automatic feed-forward methods, correspondence-based classical pipelines, and recent prompt-based vision systems. By injecting sparse point correspondences into a feed-forward stereo 3D reconstruction model through a lightweight correspondence adapter, Click3R enables users to guide the reconstruction process without test-time model fine-tuning or optimization, resolving geometric ambiguities that often cause catastrophic failures. Experiments on our curated Hard3DBench demonstrate that even a handful of correspondences can dramatically improve reconstruction quality in challenging scenarios. While Click3R has limitations (Appendix J) and failure cases (Appendix H), we hope this work inspires further exploration of correspondence prompting as a promising direction for interactive 3D reconstruction, analogous to how SAM [15] advanced interactive prompting for 2D segmentation.

Supplementary Material

We provide implementation details and training configuration (Appendix A), details on Hard3DBench construction (Appendix C), per-category analysis on the 2-view subset (Appendix D), additional experiments including training strategy ablation on all evaluation sets, stricter pose thresholds, prompt count ablation, augmentation robustness, incorrect prompts, automatic prompts, MASt3R transfer, and error distribution analysis (Appendix E), an internal analysis of how the correspondence adapter modifies encoder features and decoder attention (Appendix F), additional qualitative results (Appendix G), failure case analysis (Appendix H), licenses of the existing assets we use (Appendix I), limitation (Appendix J), and broader impacts (Appendix K).

Appendix A Implementation Details

Click3R follows the DUSt3R [44] training recipe (loss function, optimizer, data augmentation, symmetric batching) and inherits its CroCo v2 [47] ViT-Large encoder and dual asymmetric decoder. Below we detail the components specific to Click3R.

Correspondence adapter.

We insert two SAM-style [15] Two-Way Transformer adapters (depth 2, 8 heads, MLP dim 2048, embedding dim 768) between the encoder and decoder (Section 3.3). The two adapters share a single correspondence tokenizer (Section 3.2) that encodes each correspondence point as the sum of a positional encoding (random Fourier features [15]), an image identity embedding, and a pair identity embedding (vocabulary size 256). When prompts are provided, the adapted features replace the encoder output; otherwise, the adapter is bypassed and the model reduces to standard DUSt3R. The adapters and tokenizer are randomly initialized; all other weights are initialized from the CroCo pretrained checkpoint. All parameters are trained jointly end-to-end.

Training data.

We train on nine datasets, each contributing 100,000 image pairs: BlendedMVS [56], MegaDepth [19], CO3D [28], StaticThings3D [36], Waymo Open [52], ARKitScenes [2], WildRGB-D [50], Habitat [32], and ScanNet++ [57]. Validation uses held-out splits from six of these datasets with 1,000 pairs each.

Ground-truth prompt generation.

During training, correspondence prompts are generated by projecting view 1’s 3D pointmap into view 2 and accepting correspondences where the 3D distance to the nearest view 2 surface point is below 5 cm (which implicitly rejects occluded points). Per sample, 30% receive zero prompts (adapter bypassed), 40% receive 1–4, and 30% receive 5–12 correspondences.

Training configuration.

We train for 100 epochs on 4 GPUs with per-GPU batch size 16, using AdamW (β1=0.9\beta_{1}{=}0.9, β2=0.95\beta_{2}{=}0.95, weight decay 0.050.05), a learning rate of 10−410^{-4} with 10 epochs of linear warmup followed by cosine decay to 10−610^{-6}, and float16 mixed precision.

Baseline image preprocessing.

DUSt3R-family models (DUSt3R, MASt3R, Click3R) use images normalized to [−1,1][-1,1]. The VGGT and Pi3 wrappers internally denormalize images to [0,1][0,1] before forwarding to match each model’s expected input range.

Standard benchmark data.

The held-out splits are the CO3D test sequences, the ScanNet++ validation scenes, and the ARKitScenes validation videos, each processed with the DUSt3R pipeline.

Evaluation metric details.

The scale-and-shift-invariant pointmap error uses the normalization of DUSt3R: we divide the predicted pointmap by its mean point distance, shift both pointmaps by their median depth, and rescale the prediction to the median distance of the ground-truth points to their median point. We then average the per-pixel L2 distance over all valid pixels (i.e., L2 within each 3D point, mean across pixels). For mAA@θ\theta, relative camera pose is first estimated from each model’s predicted pointmaps via PnP-RANSAC (cv2.solvePnPRansac with the SQPNP solver), recovering per-view camera-to-world poses. Rotation error is the geodesic distance arccos⁡((tr⁡(Rgt⊤​Rpred)−1)/2)\arccos\!\big((\mathrm{tr}(R_{\mathrm{gt}}^{\top}R_{\mathrm{pred}})-1)/2\big) in degrees; translation error is the angular deviation between predicted and ground-truth translation directions, with sign ambiguity handled by min⁡(α,180∘−α)\min(\alpha,180^{\circ}-\alpha). mAA@θ\theta is the area under the accuracy curve of the pose error max⁡(Rerr,Terr)\max(R_{\mathrm{err}},T_{\mathrm{err}}) up to threshold θ∘\theta^{\circ}. All pairs are symmetrized (evaluated in both directions) following the standard DUSt3R protocol.

Runtime and Model Complexity.

Table 4 reports parameter counts and GPU compute times on a single NVIDIA A100 at ×224224\!\times\!224 resolution using bf16 mixed precision. The correspondence adapter adds 34.1M parameters (6.4%) over DUSt3R. When no prompts are provided, the adapter is bypassed entirely and Click3R has the same compute cost as DUSt3R (20.4 ms vs. 20.4 ms). With K=8K\!=\!8 prompts, the two-way transformer adds ∼1.0{\sim}1.0 ms of GPU compute (5%), and this overhead is nearly constant across prompt counts since the bottleneck is the fixed-size image token processing, not the number of prompts. All times report pure GPU compute (CUDA kernel time) for the model forward pass only, excluding prompt acquisition.

Appendix B Training Details

Generating Training Correspondences.

During training, we generate prompts from ground-truth 3D geometry. For each image pair with known cameras and pointmaps, we first sample the number of correspondence prompts according to a curriculum: 30% of samples use no prompts (K=0K=0), 40% use a small number of prompts (K∈[1,4]K\in[1,4]), and 30% use more prompts (K∈[5,12]K\in[5,12]). Given the sampled value of KK, we: (1) sample KK 3D points from the first view; (2) project them into both views using known intrinsics and extrinsics; (3) retain only points that are mutually visible, verified by comparing the projected 3D position against the second view’s GT pointmap within a distance threshold.

Training Protocol.

We initialize from CroCo v2 [47] pretrained weights and train all parameters end-to-end, including both the base model and the adapter. Training uses 4 GPUs, AdamW (lr=10−4\text{lr}\!=\!10^{-4}) with linear warmup and cosine decay. We train on the same dataset mixture as DUSt3R: CO3D [28], ARKitScenes [2], ScanNet++ [57], WildRGB-D [50], BlendedMVS [56], MegaDepth [19], Habitat [32], Waymo [52], and StaticThings3D [36] (100K pairs each), at 224×224224\times 224 resolution. With batch size 16 per GPU on A100s, a training step takes 0.60 s for Click3R and 0.55 s for DUSt3R (retrained), which amounts to about 234 and 215 hours for 100 epochs on 4 GPUs, with a peak memory of 29,069 and 28,731 MiB per GPU.

Appendix C Hard3DBench Details

Hard3DBench has two subsets: a 2-view stereo subset of 404 in-distribution and 300 out-of-distribution pairs, and a 5-view multi-view subset of 400 in-distribution and 300 out-of-distribution tuples. Both subsets use pretrained DUSt3R’s pose error as the difficulty signal, rather than Click3R or our retrained baseline, so the benchmark is defined independently of the methods under evaluation. They share the same source datasets: the in-distribution split uses held-out test/val splits of four DUSt3R training datasets, while the out-of-distribution split uses five datasets entirely absent from training (Table 6 reports the 2-view per-dataset statistics). DTU uses the cameras of MVSNet [55] and the depth maps rendered by Spann3R [41], 7Scenes depth is registered to the color camera as in SimpleRecon [33], ScanNet is prepared following MonST3R [58], and ETH3D following Pi3 [45].

2-view subset.

To obtain hard cases, we evaluate the pretrained DUSt3R model on up to 20,000 randomly drawn image pairs per dataset (∼{\sim}69K in-distribution, ∼{\sim}68K out-of-distribution), pre-filtering pairs with insufficient co-visibility via depth reprojection in DUSt3R’s ×224224\!\times\!224 crop space. We rank pairs by rotation error and select the top-NN worst per dataset (N=1,000N\!=\!1{,}000 for BlendedMVS, CO3D, WildRGB-D, DTU, and ETH3D; N=300N\!=\!300 for 7Scenes, NRGBD, and ScanNet). For Habitat, only the 406 of its top 1,000 pairs from scenes not used in training are kept. This yields 3,406 in-distribution and 2,900 out-of-distribution candidates. Each candidate is then classified into one or more geometric failure categories (Table 5) from ground-truth poses and depth. We uniformly subsample 404 in-distribution and 300 out-of-distribution pairs with a fixed seed.

5-view subset.

For each scene, we sample up to 30 5-frame tuples by combining stride-based windows (strides 1, 2, 5, 10, 20) with random index sampling and deduplication; tuples are kept only if all five views form a connected graph under pairwise depth-reprojection overlap ≥5%\geq 5\%. We then run DUSt3R on all C⁡(5,2)=10C(5,2){=}10 symmetrized pairs and compose them via the standard global alignment optimizer (300 iterations, msp initialization), yielding ∼16​K{\sim}16\text{K} in-distribution and ∼4​K{\sim}4\text{K} out-of-distribution candidate tuples. We rank tuples by mean pairwise rotation error and select the top-100 per in-distribution dataset (400 total) and top-60 per out-of-distribution dataset (300 total).

Difficulty for recent models.

Compared with random pairs from the same datasets with the same per-dataset counts, VGGT and Pi3 at 518 resolution drop in RRA@5 from 82.6% and 85.1% to 54.7% and 57.9% on the in-distribution pairs of the 2-view subset, and from 98.2% and 97.0% to 88.7% and 81.3% on the out-of-distribution pairs, confirming that Hard3DBench remains challenging for more recent 3D reconstruction models.

Appendix D Per-Category Analysis.

Table 7 reports mAA@30° results broken down by the five failure categories. Adding sparse correspondence prompts consistently improves performance across all categories. The largest gains are observed for geometrically challenging cases such as large viewpoint changes (+12.1) and large-baseline pairs (+8.1), where automatic matching is particularly unreliable. Substantial improvements are also seen for low-overlap pairs (+6.2) and scenes with extreme depth range (+6.6), suggesting that a few well-placed correspondences help stabilize geometric estimation. Moderate viewpoint changes benefit as well (+4.3), though the baseline model already performs relatively well in this regime. Overall, prompting improves the aggregate score from 54.6 to 61.7 (+7.1), demonstrating that sparse human-provided correspondences consistently help resolve challenging geometric configurations.

Appendix E Additional Experiments

E.1 Ablation of Training Strategies on All Evaluation Sets

Table 8 extends the training strategy ablation of Section 5 to all five evaluation sets, with the same random GT clicks for every model.

E.2 Stricter Pose Thresholds

Tables 9 and 10 extend Tables 1 and 2 with mAA@5° and mAA@15°. Against DUSt3R (retrained), the gain grows at stricter thresholds on the standard benchmark (grid oracle, +15.7+15.7 at 5° vs. +5.7+5.7 at 30°), where prompts sharpen reasonable poses, and at looser thresholds on Hard3DBench (K=8K\!=\!8, +3.6+3.6 vs. +7.7+7.7), where prompts mainly rescue large failures.

E.3 Effect of the Number of Prompts

Figure 6 shows pose accuracy as a function of the number of correspondence prompts KK on Hard3DBench. We vary K∈{0,1,2,4,8,12}K\in\{0,1,2,4,8,12\}, where K=0K\!=\!0 denotes the unprompted mode in which the adapter is bypassed entirely. All methods use ×224224\!\times\!224 input for a fair comparison.

Accuracy generally improves with KK on both splits. The effect is more pronounced on the out-of-distribution split, where even a single click (K=1K\!=\!1) yields a substantial gain. The improvement is larger on the out-of-distribution split (+11.7+11.7 pp RRA@15 from K=0K\!=\!0 to K=8K\!=\!8) than in-distribution (+8.8+8.8 pp), consistent with the base model having more room for improvement on unseen data. With K≥2K\!\geq\!2, Click3R outperforms both DUSt3R variants and VGGT on both RRA@15 and mAA@30. On the OOD split, Pi3 [45] remains stronger at every KK, likely due to its larger training data and model capacity.

E.4 Robustness to Image Augmentations

We test how well Click3R tolerates photometric perturbations by augmenting only view 2 while keeping view 1 unchanged, and measuring RRA@15° on 100 hard OOD pairs. We consider two augmentation types at two severity levels each: brightness scaling (×0.5\times 0.5, ×1.5\times 1.5) and additive Gaussian noise (σ∈{0.1,0.3}\sigma\in\{0.1,0.3\}).

As shown in Figure 7, brightness changes have negligible impact on both the unprompted and prompted models. Gaussian noise, however, exposes a clear robustness gap. At σ=0.3\sigma{=}0.3 the unprompted model drops from 21% to 6% RRA@15°, whereas the prompted model stays at 55%, suggesting that correspondence prompts provide geometric constraints that compensate for corrupted visual features.

E.5 Robustness to Incorrect Prompts

Table 11 complements the perturbation analysis of Section 5.5 with completely incorrect clicks: pose accuracy degrades monotonically as incorrect clicks replace correct ones, and all-incorrect clicks fall below using no prompts.

E.6 Automatic Prompts

We also consider scenarios without ground-truth correspondences, where we use automatic prompting from RoMa v2 [7], a state-of-the-art dense feature matcher. We run it on each image pair, rank its matches by confidence, and greedily select KK of them with a spacing of 10% of the image width in both views, so that the clicks spread over the scene. These clicks improve mAA@30 on all three sets of Table 12: with K=4K\!=\!4, from 55.9 to 58.0 on the in-distribution pairs, from 49.4 to 59.6 on the out-of-distribution pairs, and from 35.6 to 55.0 on the 100 out-of-distribution pairs with human clicks, close to the human clicks themselves (56.8).

E.7 Transfer to MASt3R

As a controlled study of whether correspondence prompting transfers to another backbone, we add the adapter to MASt3R [16] and train it end-to-end, along with a control without the adapter on the same data. Both are trained on the same nine datasets as Click3R (CO3D, ARKitScenes, ScanNet++, WildRGB-D, BlendedMVS, MegaDepth, Habitat, Waymo, and StaticThings3D), a smaller mixture than the official MASt3R recipe, so their absolute numbers are not comparable with the released model. Test-time clicks raise mAA@30 from 61.1 to 62.4 on the in-distribution pairs and from 52.1 to 54.9 on the out-of-distribution pairs (Table 13), confirming that correspondence clicks also improve performance on a different backbone.

E.8 Error Distribution Analysis

We plot per-sample distributions of reconstruction loss and pose error across the three evaluation datasets of Table 1, comparing Click3R against DUSt3R [44], MASt3R [16], VGGT [42], and Pi3X [45] at ×224224\!\times\!224 resolution.

Reconstruction loss.

Figure 8 shows the distribution of the scale-and-shift-invariant pointmap loss. Both Click3R variants (with and without prompts) have more mass near zero than DUSt3R: the fraction of samples with loss >1.0>1.0 drops from 14.9% (DUSt3R) to 11.4% (Click3R), and with loss >2.0>2.0 from 6.1% to 3.8%. Click3R without prompts already accounts for most of this reduction. VGGT [42] at ×224224\!\times\!224 shows a broader distribution (63.0% of samples exceeding loss 1.01.0), reflecting its sensitivity to input resolution.

Pose error.

Figure 9 shows the distribution of the combined pose error max⁡(Rerr,Terr)\max(R_{\text{err}},T_{\text{err}}). Click3R with prompts produces a sharper peak near 0∘0^{\circ} and a shorter tail than all baselines. The fraction of pairs with pose error exceeding 15∘15^{\circ} drops from 9.4% (DUSt3R) to 6.1% (Click3R without prompts) and further to 2.8% (Click3R with prompts)—a 3.4×3.4{\times} reduction. At the 30∘30^{\circ} threshold, the failure rate decreases from 4.7% to 0.8%. The reduction is concentrated in the tail rather than a uniform shift of the distribution, indicating that prompts primarily resolve the hardest cases.

Appendix F What Does the Adapter Do?

We examine how the correspondence adapter modifies encoder features and how this affects downstream decoder attention.

Feature modification.

Figure 10 visualizes the relative change in each token’s feature vector before and after the adapter (∥Δ​f∥/∥f∥\lVert\Delta f\rVert/\lVert f\rVert) for a representative pair with K=8K\!=\!8 prompts. The adapter does not apply a uniform transformation: feature changes are largest near the prompt locations (cyan dots), although every token is modified.

Effect on decoder cross-attention.

Figure 11 shows how prompts reshape the decoder’s cross-view attention. For three query patches in view 1 (green crosses), we visualize where each query attends in view 2 with and without prompts. Without prompts, cross-attention is diffuse and sometimes focuses on incorrect regions. With prompts, attention shifts toward the geometrically correct correspondences.

Appendix G More Qualitative Visualizations

Figure 13 presents additional qualitative comparisons on challenging pairs. For each example, we show the input pair with correspondence clicks, the ground-truth reconstruction, and the predictions of DUSt3R, Pi3, and Click3R. These cases illustrate scenarios where at least one baseline produces a noticeably incorrect reconstruction. For instance, DUSt3R may fail on a pair where Pi3 succeeds, or vice versa. Click3R with sparse correspondence clicks consistently recovers geometry close to the ground truth across all shown examples. The clicked correspondences converge to consistent 3D locations in the Click3R reconstruction, confirming that the adapter successfully leverages sparse correspondences to resolve geometric ambiguities that affect different baselines in different ways.

Appendix H Failure Cases

Figure 14 shows four representative failure modes of Click3R. Each panel shows the input image pair (left), the ground-truth reconstruction (middle), and the Click3R reconstruction with clicks (right).

(a) Few overlap. When the two views share little or no visual overlap, the model must hallucinate the relative geometry from appearance alone. In this ScanNet++ example the views observe disjoint parts of a room; comparing the ground truth with the Click3R output reveals a severely misaligned reconstruction. Without co-visible content, correspondence clicks cannot anchor the two views—this is a fundamental limitation of pairwise reconstruction.

(b) Heavy rotation. Extreme viewpoint changes (>90∘>90^{\circ}) remain an unsolved challenge. In this ARKitScenes pair, the Click3R reconstruction remains geometrically distorted compared to the ground truth. While clicks can reduce error in moderate-rotation cases (Table 7), very heavy rotations overwhelm the model’s capacity to reconcile drastically different visual appearances.

(c) Large-scale scenes. For outdoor scenes with large spatial extent (MegaDepth), correspondence clicks correctly constrain geometry near the clicked regions, but distant structures still exhibit bending and deformation—visible here as warped sky and distorted building facades far from the click locations. A small number of clicks cannot regularize the entire scene when the depth range spans tens of meters.

(d) Ambiguous correspondences. On textureless or repetitive surfaces, correspondences themselves become ambiguous. In this ARKitScenes bathroom scene with featureless marble walls and white surfaces, a click on one location is visually indistinguishable from many others, providing little geometric information. The Click3R reconstruction remains distorted compared to the ground truth, and clicks offer negligible improvement.

Appendix J Limitations

Although correspondence prompts are ideally injected into a frozen pretrained model, we find that training the base model [44] end-to-end with the adapter is necessary in practice, incurring nontrivial training cost. Partly due to this cost, our experiments focus on two-view reconstruction; extending to multi-view models [45, 42, 53, 40] with trajectory prompts across NN views is an important direction.

Architecturally, the adapter treats correspondences as soft feature conditioning via cross-attention rather than enforcing hard geometric constraints. Although eight correspondences suffice to determine relative pose algebraically [8], the adapter cannot replicate such reasoning: it modulates all image tokens through learned attention at a single injection point, and this signal is progressively diluted across twelve subsequent decoder cross-attention blocks. Deeper injection at multiple decoder layers and explicit geometric reasoning modules may be worth future inquiry to help close this gap.

Finally, due to computational constraints, the model is trained only at a resolution of 224224px in a stereo setting, although it has demonstrated multi-view capability through global alignment. In addition, prompts must be co-visible in both views, so the two inputs need a shared visible region; non-overlapping inputs could be connected through intermediate views by chaining correspondences. Severely incorrect correspondences can degrade reconstruction quality (Table 11).

Appendix K Broader Impacts

Our work enables more efficient 3D reconstruction from sparse user-provided correspondences. By allowing a small number of clicks to anchor pairwise reconstruction, Click3R can lower the barrier to 3D capture in diverse, in-the-wild scenes, which may benefit downstream applications such as robotics, AR/VR content creation, and scientific imaging where dense ground-truth geometry is unavailable. Our model and benchmark are built from publicly available datasets (CO3D, ScanNet++, ARKitScenes, BlendedMVS, MegaDepth, Habitat, WildRGB-D, Waymo, and standard evaluation benchmarks), and therefore do not raise privacy concerns. While our algorithm itself is scene-agnostic and does not introduce explicit bias, the underlying training datasets may reflect societal or geographic biases present in the source data (e.g., predominantly indoor scenes from North American buildings, or object categories skewed toward consumer products). We encourage future work to investigate and mitigate such biases when deploying systems trained on these data.
